review.headline: A winning piece up spoiled by a lagging king

sections.text: You punished your opponent's opening mistake in Petrov's Defense quickly. After 4.Qe2 d5 5.d3, Black failed to protect their knight and gave you a clean piece with 7.dxe4 dxe4 8.Nfd2. You were up a bishop for a pawn, but with Black's rook immediately seizing the e-file with 8...Re8, your primary task was securing your king.

Instead of developing pieces to block the center, you chose 9.g3, opening up weaknesses along the central files. Black missed the sharpest continuation and tried 9...Bb4, which set up a discovered attack on your queen and a pin against your knight on d2. You pushed the bishop back with 10.c3 Bc5, regaining the upper hand.

The decisive misstep came right after. You played 11.Bg2, but leaving your king on e1 opposite the rook proved fatal against 11...e3. When the pawn broke through, 12.O-O exf2+ shattered your position and forced an early resignation.

review.turning_point: On move 11, playing 11.Bg2 allowed the crushing central break 11...e3, turning an extra piece into a collapsing king position.
review.focus: Prioritize rapid development to shield your king on open central files instead of slow fianchetto setups like 9.g3.

review.headline: A sharp Petrov that ended before it truly began

sections.text: You stepped into Petrov's Defense with 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6, quickly capturing the central pawn with 3.Nxe5. Black responded immediately in the center with 3...d5, giving you a clear opportunity to take control with the simple capture 4.exd5.

Instead, you opted to support your center with 4.f3??. This weakened your kingside and gave away your advantage, shifting the evaluation from +1.2 to -0.7. Black could have looked to exploit this immediately with 4...Nxe4 5.g3.

Black missed that chance and played 4...Bc5?, swinging the position back in your favor (+0.8). However, the game ended right here after just four moves with your resignation, even though the position remained completely playable.

review.turning_point: Playing 4.f3?? compromised your kingside, though Black immediately made a mistake of their own with 4...Bc5? before the sudden resignation.
review.focus: Avoid weakening moves like 4.f3 early in the opening; instead, look to capture free central material with 4.exd5 to maintain the initiative.

review.headline: A sharp Petrov transition leads to a winning pawn grab and a time-trouble finish

sections.text: You handled Petrov's Defense solidly, completing development and castling smoothly. After 15.Bxf6, you responded accurately with 15...Nxf6! to keep your piece coordination intact. When White played 19.Qh4, stepping the queen away in a discovered attack against your bishop on e6, you didn't panic and immediately struck in the center with 19...dxc4!, winning a clean pawn after 20.bxc4 Bxc4.

You consolidated your advantage nicely by trading rooks after White's 26.Qxf3? with 26...Re1+ 27.Rxe1 Qxe1+. However, with a winning position on move 28, you hesitated: 28...Qa1?? missed the cleaner 28...Bxd4, which would have kept all your threats alive. Luckily White gave the pawn right back with 29.a3??, allowing 29...Qxd4.

The endgame remained favorable, but 31...c5?? needlessly surrendered your passed c-pawn after 32.Qb8+ Kh7 33.Qxb7. Once the queens came off with 33...Qxb7 34.Bxb7, White's bishop locked down your advanced pawn on c3. The game simplified into an opposite-colored bishop ending, and you took the win when White flagged on move 43.
